title: Many streams
hook: the panth holds many orders and schools, each with its own emphasis

segments.voice: Yesterday the code closed: a shared way of life for a scattered people. Your line was one way, many places. This week ran from children and work to humility and joy. Which piece of the code stayed with you? Day one thousand three hundred two.

A big city gurdwara on a holiday morning. Near the door stands a man in deep blue, his turban wound high and ringed with steel. Inside, a young student reads from the Granth slowly, every syllable placed like a stone in a wall. In the kitchen, an older man in plain white washes pots and says almost nothing all day. Upstairs, a group has been singing since before dawn. They all bowed to the same Granth on the way in. They didn't all learn their ways in the same place. For weeks now we've been reading the code that holds the panth together. Today we start meeting the streams that run inside it.
screen: `A MAN IN DEEP BLUE AT THE DOOR.` → `A STUDENT READING SLOWLY.` → `A QUIET MAN AT THE POTS.`

segments.voice: The word for a stream like that is sampardaa: a tradition handed on, teacher to student, with its own way of doing things. Over the coming weeks you'll meet several. Some are orders of renunciants who look after shrines. Some are scholars who wrote commentaries. One is known for quiet service, one keeps the old martial life on horseback, one teaches careful recitation, one sings through the night. Each puts its weight on a different thing. And each, in its own telling, traces its line back to the Gurus. Now a line from the Gurus that fits the moment. In the hymn Sikhs call Sohila, sung at night, Guru Nanak speaks of six schools, six teachers and six teachings. Then, in paraphrase: but the Teacher of teachers is one, appearing in many forms. He was speaking about the schools of his own day, not about Sikh orders that came later. Still, the shape of the thought helps here. Many ways of teaching; one source. Two honest things belong next to that. First, Sikhs hold a range of views about these streams: how close each stands to the Khalsa's code, where an emphasis becomes a difference. Some of those questions are still argued, and this path won't settle them. Second, a stream is not a wall. A Sikh can learn kirtan from one, pronunciation from another, and service from a third, and come home to the same congregation. So the plan for these weeks is simple. Meet each one on its own terms, hear what it cares about most, and rank none of them.
screen: `SAMPARDAA: A TRADITION HANDED ON.` · `EACH LEANS ON SOMETHING DIFFERENT.` · `SOHILA: SIX TEACHERS, ONE TEACHER.` · `A STREAM IS NOT A WALL.` · then, large: `MANY STREAMS, ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one new stream. Settle, and breathe. From the few you heard about today, the shrine keepers, the scholars, the servers, the riders, the readers, the night singers, choose one that you know least about. Hold just its outline in mind, without judging it. Breathe in, and let the question form: what does this one care about most? Breathe out, and leave the answer open. You'll meet it properly soon. The bell holds the time.
Sampardaa. A tradition handed on from teacher to student, with its own emphasis. The panth holds several, and each traces itself to the Gurus. Today's word.

Your line: many streams, one guru. Today, when you meet someone who does a shared thing differently from you, ask them where they learned it, and listen to the whole answer. Day one thousand three hundred two.

howItsDone: Sikhs learn from more than one sampardaa: a congregation may hear kirtan in one style, katha from a scholar of another school, and recitation taught by a third, while all bow to the Guru Granth Sahib.

fork.setup: Guru Nanak names six schools, six teachers and six teachings. what does he say next?
options: that one of the six is right and the rest are wrong.
that the Teacher of teachers is one, in many forms.
that teachers aren't needed at all.
fork.reveal: the Teacher of teachers is one, appearing in many forms. many ways of teaching; one source.

original.note: Punjabi: a tradition or school handed down from teacher to student.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Sikh panth is one uniform group.
what it means: it holds several sampardaas, each with its own emphasis, each tracing itself to the Gurus.
what a scholar hears: how each stream relates to the Khalsa's code is still discussed among Sikhs, and the answers differ stream by stream.
recall: the one who leads the band
